"executive_summary": "This prospective single-center cohort study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length influences six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes after successful drug-eluting stent (DES)–based percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). A total of 235 consecutive patients who underwent successful CTO PCI with DES from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital were divided into a long CTO group (angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm, n=159) and a short CTO group (<30 mm, n=76). Baseline characteristics were largely similar, with prior PCI more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group; in-hospital intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Angiographic follow-up at 6–12 months was obtained in 99 of 159 long CTO patients (62%) and 45 of 76 short CTO patients (59%), and six-month angiographic outcomes—including binary restenosis, in-stent restenosis, late loss, and mean diameter stenosis—were statistically similar between groups, though binary restenosis showed a numerically higher trend in the long CTO group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12). Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; 21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13), total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), and myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71) did not differ between groups. However, repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05), predominantly as target vessel revascularization (TVR; 16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52–11.8, p<0.05). The authors conclude that, despite successful DES-based CTO PCI, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, although this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized single-center design, small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration, and calls for larger long-term studies. This work contributes to the understanding of lesion-length–related prognostic factors in the DES era and supports continued attention to long CTO lesions as a predictor of repeat revascularization, while noting that the absence of differences in hard endpoints may reflect reduced myocardial viability and collateral development in long CTO lesions.",

summary.executive_summary: This prospective single-center cohort study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length influences six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes after successful drug-eluting stent (DES)–based percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Baseline characteristics were largely similar, with prior PCI more frequent in the long CTO group and bifurcation lesions more frequent in the short CTO group; in-hospital intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Angiographic follow-up at 6–12 months was obtained in 99 of 159 long CTO patients (62%) and 45 of 76 short CTO patients (59%), and six-month angiographic outcomes—including binary restenosis, in-stent restenosis, late loss, and mean diameter stenosis—were statistically similar between groups, though binary restenosis showed a numerically higher trend in the long CTO group (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.12). Over two years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE; 21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13), total death (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43), cardiac death (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45), and myocardial infarction (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71) did not differ between groups. However, repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05), predominantly as target vessel revascularization (TVR; 16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52–11.8, p<0.05). The authors conclude that, despite successful DES-based CTO PCI, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, although this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized single-center design, small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration, and calls for larger long-term studies. This work contributes to the understanding of lesion-length–related prognostic factors in the DES era and supports continued attention to long CTO lesions as a predictor of repeat revascularization, while noting that the absence of differences in hard endpoints may reflect reduced myocardial viability and collateral development in long CTO lesions.

Executive Summary
This prospective single-center cohort study investigated whether chronic total occlusion (CTO) lesion length influences six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes after successful drug-eluting stent (DES)–based percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). However, repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05), predominantly as target vessel revascularization (TVR; 16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). The authors conclude that, despite successful DES-based CTO PCI, long CTO lesions are associated with a higher rate of repeat revascularization, although this did not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. The study acknowledges limitations including its non-randomized single-center design, small sample size, lack of routine follow-up angiography, and insufficient follow-up duration, and calls for larger long-term studies. This work contributes to the understanding of lesion-length–related prognostic factors in the DES era and supports continued attention to long CTO lesions as a predictor of repeat revascularization, while noting that the absence of differences in hard endpoints may reflect reduced myocardial viability and collateral development in long CTO lesions.

Research Context
Successful CTO PCI is associated with improved clinical outcomes compared with failed CTO PCI. DES and device development have reduced restenosis and adverse events after PCI. Long coronary artery lesions are a worse prognostic factor after PCI. CTO procedural success rates remain lower than non-CTO patients. CTO long-term outcomes are affected by clinical risk factors and baseline lesion characteristics. Lesion length is a major predictor of MACE and restenosis after DES stent implantation. There are no definite answers regarding CTO PCI outcomes according to CTO lesion length, especially in the DES era.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central research question concerns whether CTO lesion length impacts six-month angiographic and two-year clinical outcomes after successful CTO PCI. The primary hypothesis was that long CTO lesions would be associated with worse angiographic and clinical outcomes due to worse baseline risk factors. The authors hypothesized that the long CTO group has worse clinical risk factors such as prior MI and PCI. The authors hypothesized that newer-generation DES use was dominant in the short CTO group. The authors predicted that paclitaxel-eluting stents were frequently used in the long CTO group. The predicted outcome was that long CTO lesions would predict higher repeat revascularization.

Methodological Details
The study enrolled 235 consecutive CTO patients who underwent successful PCI with DES. Patients were enrolled from November 2004 to October 2010 at Korea University Guro Hospital. The study was conducted at the Cardiovascular Center of Korea University Guro Hospital in Seoul, South Korea. Patients were divided into long CTO (≥30 mm) and short CTO (<30 mm) groups by lesion length. The long CTO group comprised 159 patients with angiographic lesion length ≥30 mm. The short CTO group comprised 76 patients with angiographic lesion length <30 mm. The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. CTO was defined as complete coronary obstruction with TIMI flow grade 0 and estimated duration ≥3 months. Only de novo lesions were included, and CTO due to in-stent restenosis was excluded. Loading doses of clopidogrel (300–600 mg) and aspirin (200–300 mg) were administered before the index procedure. Maintenance dual antiplatelet therapy comprised aspirin (100 mg) and clopidogrel (75 mg).

Procedures And Architectures
PCI procedures were performed with current guidelines using standard techniques. Various guidewires were used to cross the CTO lesion. Atheroablative devices were not utilized in the procedures. Mostly simple pre-dilation with balloon was performed to accommodate the stent. All PCI was performed using DES, with the DES type decided by the operator. Procedural success was defined as final diameter stenosis <30% and TIMI grade ≥2. QCA parameters were measured before PCI, immediately after PCI, and 6 months after the procedure. The primary angiographic endpoint was binary restenosis at 6–12 months. Secondary angiographic endpoints included ISR, mean diameter stenosis, MLD, and late loss at 6 months. Two-year follow-up data were collected by face-to-face interview, medical record review, and/or telephone contact. The primary clinical endpoint was MACE, defined as total death, recurrent MI, and revascularization. Secondary clinical endpoints included death, MI, repeat PCI, TLR, TVR, and non-TVR.

Key Results
A total of 235 CTO patients were divided into long CTO (n=159) and short CTO (n=76) groups. Prior PCI was more frequent in the long CTO group than the short CTO group. Bifurcation lesions were more frequent in the short CTO group than the long CTO group. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group than the short CTO group. Angiographic follow-up at 6–12 months was obtained in 99 of 159 long CTO patients (62%). Angiographic follow-up at 6–12 months was obtained in 45 of 76 short CTO patients (59%). The incidence of ISR was 33.3% in the long CTO group versus 26.6% in the short CTO group (p=0.42). The incidence of binary restenosis was 19.1% in the long CTO group versus 8.8% in the short CTO group (p=0.12). Late loss was 0.65 ± 0.82 mm in the long CTO group versus 0.46 ± 0.56 mm in the short CTO group (p=0.13). Total death was 3.1% in the long CTO group versus 5.2% in the short CTO group (p=0.43). Cardiac death was 1.2% in the long CTO group versus 2.6% in the short CTO group (p=0.45). Myocardial infarction was 1.8% in the long CTO group versus 2.6% in the short CTO group (p=0.71).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR in the long CTO group did not translate into differences in hard endpoints such as mortality. The long CTO group showed numerically higher binary restenosis (19.1% vs. 8.8%, p=0.118). The presence of less myocardial viability and collateral channels may lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis. Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006). Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52–11.8, p<0.05). The higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR supports the hypothesis of higher restenosis in long CTO lesions over time.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study was not a randomized study and was a single-center registry with prospectively collected data. Baseline clinical, lesion, and procedural characteristics were slightly different between the two groups. Newer-generation DES use was frequent in the short CTO group, and first-generation stents were frequent in the long CTO group. Follow-up coronary angiography was not routinely performed in all patients. The sample size was relatively small, limiting power to detect differences in angiographic events. The two-year follow-up period was not long enough to evaluate long-term safety and efficacy. Unmeasured confounders and analytical bias could remain despite strict statistical adjustment. Well-developed collaterals and myocardial viability could influence ischemic symptoms and confounders.

Claims
Long CTO lesions are associated with a higher incidence of repeat PCI and TVR after successful DES-based CTO PCI, but this does not translate into differences in hard clinical endpoints such as mortality or cardiac death. Repeat PCI was significantly higher in the long CTO group (18.8% vs. 7.8%, p<0.05). TVR was significantly higher in the long CTO group (16.3% vs. 6.5%, p<0.05). Long CTO was an independent predictor of repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006). Long CTO was an independent predictor of TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52–11.8, p<0.05). MACE did not differ between groups (21.3% vs. 13.1%, p=0.13). Total death did not differ between groups (3.1% vs. 5.2%, p=0.43). Cardiac death did not differ between groups (1.2% vs. 2.6%, p=0.45). MI did not differ between groups (1.8% vs. 2.6%, p=0.71). Long CTO lesions should be considered a predictor of repeat revascularization in the DES era. The higher TVR incidence did not translate into individual critical hard endpoints such as mortality. Less myocardial viability and collateral channels may lessen the harmful physiologic effect of restenosis. Larger long-term studies are required to reach a final conclusion.
Successful CTO PCI with DES is similarly safe between long and short CTO lesions, with no significant differences in in-hospital complications except intimal dissection. In-hospital complications were similar between the two groups except intimal dissection. Intimal dissection was more frequent in the long CTO group. Procedural safety and efficacy were similar between the two groups during hospitalization. The long CTO group had more frequent intimal dissection, suggesting more complex recanalization. The long CTO group had more frequent false channel wire passage. Long CTO PCI is similarly safe as short CTO PCI despite successful DES implantation. Intimal dissection may reflect more aggressive recanalization in long CTO lesions.

Data And Code Availability
The study data were collected prospectively at Korea University Guro Hospital.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Multivariate logistic regression identified long CTO as an independent predictor of repeat PCI. The analysis adjusted for sex, age, hypertension, DM, chronic kidney disease, prior PCI, and bifurcation lesion. The six-month angiographic outcomes were statistically similar between the two groups.

Ethical Considerations
The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at Korea University Guro Hospital. All patients provided informed consent to participate in the study. The paper is a bioRxiv preprint not certified by peer review. The paper is available under a CC-BY 4.0 International license.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 demonstrates baseline clinical and angiographic characteristics of the two groups. Table 2 shows procedural and in-hospital complications, with intimal dissection more frequent in the long CTO group. Table 3 summarizes clinical outcomes for the 2-year follow-up period. Table 4 shows predictors for repeat PCI and TVR, with long CTO as an independent predictor. Table 5 presents six-month angiographic outcomes, with binary restenosis higher in the long CTO group.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is that long CTO lesions predict higher repeat PCI and TVR after successful DES-based CTO PCI. 2. The strongest evidence is the multivariate finding that long CTO independently predicts repeat PCI (OR 4.26, CI 1.53–11.9, p=0.006) and TVR (OR 4.23, CI 1.52–11.8, p<0.05). 3. The future path is larger long-term studies with routine follow-up angiography to reach a final conclusion.
